author_rationale: Familial medication preferences and genetically related behaviors may affect actual use. A residual familial pathway is retained beyond the other represented nodes.
Age and family support may affect medication choice under the same symptoms. The proposed effect concerns these demographic components.
Established psychiatric conditions may affect risk perception, self-medication and adherence through pathways beyond symptoms and healthcare contacts.
Underlying renal, hepatic or other conditions may affect analgesic choice and restrictions even when indications are similar.
Healthcare contacts, consultation and access before target medication use may affect actual use. Contacts after X are outside this pathway.
Prior or concurrent treatments may substitute for, combine with or restrict target medication use. Treatments initiated after X are outside this pathway.
Psychosocial conditions may affect child screening, healthcare contacts and diagnostic recording. Y is a recorded outcome; this pathway concerns ascertainment.
Child physical illness may increase pediatric contacts and referrals, affecting outcome recording. This does not establish a direct effect of common infections on ASD.
Familial background and family characteristics may overlap. Distinct components and a causal pathway have not been specified.
Ancestry-region associations do not establish that familial background changes geography. A migration mechanism and its timing have not been specified.
Family healthcare beliefs and illness experience may affect maternal care seeking and preventive examinations. This is retained as a shared-background assumption.
Family treatment experience and medication beliefs may affect treatment choice. The pathway concerns shared background, without attributing an effect to every genetic measure.
Familial aggregation or gene-environment association does not establish an independent direct effect. A mechanism beyond socioeconomic and residential selection has not been specified.
Genetically related lactation capacity and breastfeeding propensity may affect feeding. Twin studies support this possibility without identifying a direct effect of a particular gene.
Age, marital status and household composition may affect employment and income. The pathway is restricted to these demographic components.

Socioeconomic conditions may affect subsequent marriage and reproduction, but C02 combines fixed attributes and changing household structure. Timing is insufficiently resolved for a general reverse edge.
Early-onset, persistent psychiatric conditions may affect marital stability and household formation when they precede the relevant household changes.
Maternal age and related demographic characteristics may affect chronic and metabolic disease through biological pathways beyond the represented socioeconomic and behavioral nodes.
Previous childbearing may change household composition and co-residence. The pathway concerns household structure, excluding fixed attributes such as age or group background.
Household composition and population context may affect occupational, residential and household exposures beyond differences in income.
Income may affect migration, and earlier geography may affect income. C04 also includes calendar time; components and timing are insufficiently separated to fix a direction.
Geography may affect socioeconomic conditions, while socioeconomic conditions may affect migration. Earlier geography and current residence are insufficiently separated to fix a direction.
C03 describes socioeconomic position in the target pregnancy and cannot cause completed reproductive history. Earlier socioeconomic circumstances require a separate time reference.
Previous childbearing may affect current employment and income through caregiving demands and career interruption. This pathway does not imply an effect on completed education.
Affordability, insurance and medication access may affect treatment choice beyond what visit counts capture.
Family resources may affect early development through learning opportunities and caregiving. Cash-intervention evidence offers partial support without establishing an effect on ASD.
Psychiatric conditions cannot change calendar time. Health-selective migration is possible, but its temporal relationship with psychiatric conditions is unspecified.
Geography and period may affect maternal health through pathogens, food supply and sanitation not represented as separate nodes.
Geographical and temporal differences in obstetric services and delivery practice may affect perinatal outcomes beyond maternal visit counts.
Geographical and temporal differences in pathogens and sanitation may affect childhood infection beyond specific chemical exposures.
Established psychiatric conditions may affect physical and metabolic health through neuroendocrine pathways not fully mediated by behaviors or medications. This is a working assumption.
Early-onset, persistent neuropsychiatric conditions may affect reproductive decisions and pregnancy processes when they clearly precede the relevant previous pregnancy.
Established neuropsychiatric conditions may affect later stress responses, smoking and alcohol use. The assumed ordering places established conditions before subsequent behaviors.
Stress or behavior during the target pregnancy cannot cause a previously established psychiatric condition. Earlier cumulative exposures require a separate temporal definition.
Environmental exposure has not been shown to precede established psychiatric conditions in these definitions. Current pregnancy exposure cannot explain a prior condition in reverse time.
Psychiatric symptoms persisting postpartum may affect breastfeeding intention, ability and continuation. Historical diagnoses alone do not establish current symptoms.
Psychiatric symptoms persisting postpartum may affect childhood infection through caregiving and health management. Cohort evidence supports this pathway but allows residual confounding.
Persistent maternal psychiatric conditions may affect development through early interactions and caregiving. Shared genetic associations alone do not establish this pathway.
C06 does not separately define health before previous pregnancies. Health in or immediately before the target pregnancy cannot cause completed obstetric history.
Previous pregnancies may leave persistent weight retention, pelvic-floor injury or other health changes. Predictive associations with later chronic disease alone do not establish causation.
Maternal autoantibodies may cross the placenta and cause neonatal skin or immune abnormalities. This concerns specific immune components, not every BMI or chronic-disease component.
Previous pregnancy or childbirth may leave persistent pelvic or pelvic-floor pain that becomes an indication for target medication use.
Transient pregnancy infection or pain does not establish a postpartum breastfeeding effect. Persistence into lactation has not been specified.
Pregnancy infections may affect early child health through vertical transmission or immune pathways. This does not extend to every pain indication.
Infection-related inflammation does not establish a change in the post-acetaminophen response. A drug-specific interaction mechanism is lacking.

author_rationale: Parity-related pathways are represented through household composition, current maternal health and perinatal health. No additional direct mechanism is specified.
Prior obstetric history can mark background risk represented through maternal health, perinatal health and family resources. Prediction alone does not support an additional direct edge.
Smoking, alcohol use and living conditions before treatment decisions may affect medication choice and adherence.
Active smoking is represented in C09 and cannot be duplicated in C12 to create an edge. Other behavioral and environmental components lack specified timing.
External exposures may affect subsequent stress or behavior, but specific components and temporal ordering are unresolved.
Smoking, alcohol use and psychosocial support persisting into lactation may affect lactation and breastfeeding. Pregnancy-only behaviors cannot be assumed to persist.
Known occupational or environmental exposures may trigger consultation, screening and monitoring before symptoms arise. This is a preventive care-seeking pathway.
Breastfeeding advice and support during antenatal care may affect initiation and duration. The pathway is limited to contacts providing those services.
Specific serotonergic medications may affect lactation onset when their effects persist through delivery or breastfeeding.
Perinatal antibiotics may affect infant microbial colonization within relevant drug classes and exposure windows.
Evidence supports offspring developmental effects of particular pregnancy medications, including valproate. This does not imply a uniform effect of all concomitant medications.
Some concomitant medications may induce or inhibit metabolic pathways and alter post-acetaminophen responses. Such changes need not increase toxicity.
Cohort evidence links prenatal PFAS exposure with shorter breastfeeding duration. This candidate pathway remains chemical-specific, with limited mechanistic and causal evidence.
General oxidative stress from pollution does not establish an interaction with the post-acetaminophen response. A pollutant-specific drug interaction has not been specified.

author_rationale: Sucking, swallowing or regulatory difficulties preceding a feeding outcome may affect feeding. Later-recognized developmental problems cannot establish an earlier breastfeeding effect.
Early central nervous system infection may affect subsequent development. The pathway requires infection before developmental assessment and does not extend to all infections or allergic conditions.
Developmental abnormalities may affect later health, but this reverses the ordering of the proposed forward pathway. Separate early and late nodes are required.
Post-exposure biological and pharmacological responses may affect the subsequent developmental environment. This is a candidate mechanism, not established acetaminophen neurotoxicity.
